items.title: Enhancing the Role of Digital Health Navigators With Lived Experience: AI-Assisted Conavigation for Safety, Support, and Engagement
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) expands across mental health services, questions arise about whether it can replace digital health navigators (DHNs), including those with lived experience. The DHN role generally resists automation because lived experience deepens specific dimensions that AI cannot replicate. Drawing on emerging evidence of AI's limitations in contextual reasoning, cultural sensitivity, and clinical safety, the authors identify where DHNs with lived experience are least substitutable: real-world knowledge of services, cultural grounding in the communities they serve, and relational trust. A practical model is also outlined in which AI augments DHN workflows through triage, documentation, and engagement monitoring.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: Epistemological Friction in Artificial Intelligence Use among Humanities Faculty and Students in Western Mindanao, Philippines
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has entered higher education faster than institutional policy can regulate it, a gap visible in Philippine humanities programs, where interpretive originality and authorial voice are central to disciplinary practice. Humanities programs in regional, resource-constrained Philippine settings remain largely absent from the AI-adoption literature, a gap this study addressed by examining AI adoption, perceived usefulness and ease of use, perceived risk, AI literacy, and behavioral intention among humanities faculty and undergraduate students at a state university in Zamboanga City, Philippines, where no institutional AI policy exists. A convergent mixed-methods design combined survey data from 200 students and 23 faculty with ten in-depth interviews; quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, multiple regression, and Welch's t-test, while qualitative data underwent reflexive thematic analysis, integrated through joint display analysis. Students used AI moderately and selectively, favoring comprehension and organization over original composition. Faculty reported higher AI familiarity than students but markedly lower classroom use (M = 3.59 versus M = 2.67), a pattern proposed here as epistemological friction: principled disciplinary resistance rather than technical inability. Both groups perceived high risk, yet risk predicted only the intention to limit AI use (r = .531, p < .001), not the intention to discontinue it (r = .047, ns), producing concealed adoption tentatively labeled a shadow AI ecosystem. Perceived usefulness (β = .427) and ease of use (β = .365) were the strongest predictors of continued use, while students significantly outperformed faculty in AI literacy (d = -0.943), reversing the assumed top-down transmission of competence. AI acceptance here was shaped as much by disciplinary values and unclear institutional guidance as by usefulness or ease of use, supporting tiered governance, faculty development addressing disciplinary and ethical concerns, and structured reverse mentoring to narrow the literacy gap and reduce concealed AI use.

items.title: EpiWorld: Grounding LLM Policy Agents in Epidemiological World Models
items.abstract: Epidemic intervention policies are textual artefacts that human decision-makers interpret, justify, and revise through natural language, making large language models a natural candidate for epidemic policy reasoning. A naive LLM, however, lacks the epidemic dynamics needed to project intervention consequences, the quantitative surveillance signals required to assess severity, and the institutional constraints that define admissible actions. We present EpiWorld, a closed-loop framework that grounds an LLM policy actor in a learned action-conditioned epidemiological world model and a tiered skill library of public-health protocols, surveillance tools, and adaptive lessons accumulated through after-action analysis. Given a candidate intervention, the world model predicts regional epidemic evolution and enables fast counterfactual rollouts that provide feedback for policy selection and refinement. Outcomes of simulated futures are distilled into reusable lessons while protocol constraints remain fixed, allowing the decision process to improve without sacrificing interpretability or controllability. We evaluate both the world model and the end-to-end framework on retrospective COVID-19 and Influenza datasets: the world model achieves the best out-of-distribution Peak-MAE among all forecasting baselines, and the closed-loop framework reduces cumulative hospitalisation by up to 59% across datasets and by an average of ~16% across six LLM backbones, outperforming reinforcement-learning and optimal-control policy baselines.
topics: Mathematical and Theoretical Epidemiology and Ecology Models

items.title: Ergonomic Opportunistic Networks: A Human-Centric Architecture for Adaptive Resource Orchestration
items.abstract: Opportunistic networks acquire external communication, computation, sensing, storage, and service resources as mission requirements evolve. Prior research has developed human-mobility models, context-aware routing, trust mechanisms, and adaptive resource-management approaches, but these contributions address narrower decision scopes and do not by themselves provide an ergonomics-guided process for governing heterogeneous Helpers throughout mission execution. This paper formalises Ergonomic Opportunistic Networks (ErOppNets) as a technology-independent extension of mission-driven opportunistic networks in which ergonomics serves as a design compass for selecting and adapting technologies, policies, resources, and participation mechanisms to support human factors and ergonomics goals alongside mission performance. ErOppNets integrate human-centric, context-aware, trust-aware, and resource-aware decisions across discovery, assessment, admission, role allocation, monitoring, reassessment, reconfiguration, replacement, and release. A multidimensional orchestration model formalises Helper selection, while the ErOppNet Adaptive Orchestration (EAO) procedure translates the model into operational decisions. The evaluation compares six policies across nominal, dynamic, adversarial, resource scarcity, failure, and scalability scenarios using 100 paired random seeds per primary comparative configuration, complemented by separate parameter-sensitivity analyses. Under nominal conditions, EAO and Static Multidimensional (SM) selection achieved 100 per cent mission completion; relative to SM, EAO reduced mean configuration churn by 60.0 per cent. Across dynamic conditions and external populations up to 2000 entities, EAO preserved mission feasibility while balancing utility, stability, trust requirements, and adversarial exposure. The results support ErOppNets as a human-centric, adaptive, and technology-independent model for intelligent opportunistic network management.

items.title: Ethical Labour Governance in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Automation
items.abstract: The fast adoption of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) and automation is changing how organisations operate and govern labour. The conventional Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) models, which are predominantly directed toward philanthropy, cannot deal with emerging issues like the bias in algorithms, labor displacement, online surveillance, and risks of data governance. In this chapter, the author discusses the use of ethical labour governance in AI-driven workplaces and recommends a governance framework based on CSR, which incorporates responsible AI, algorithmic responsibility, and strategies aimed at inclusive workforce transition. The chapter provides insights into the conceptual analysis and case-driven knowledge to define governance mechanisms such as standards of transparency, reskilling programs, and multi-stakeholder control. In the study, the author has placed utmost importance on responsible automation as a means of balancing technological innovation and the dignity of workers, social equality, and long-term sustainability.

items.title: Evaluating LLM-as-a-Judge Beyond Score Alignment: A Psychometric Analysis of Residual Judging Difficulty
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as automatic judges, with validity typically assessed via alignment with human scores. However, aggregate agreement fails to reveal whether humans and LLMs find the same evaluation cases difficult. In this paper, we study this problem in summarization evaluation from a psychometric perspective. We fit Many-Facet Rasch Models separately to human and LLM ratings to decompose scores into latent summary quality, rater severity, dimension severity, and rating-scale thresholds. Building on this decomposition, we define residual hardness as a model-adjusted measure of judging difficulty and compare whether human and LLM judges share the same hardness structure. Across 17 open-weight LLM judges on SummEval, we find that moderate alignment in latent summary quality does not imply alignment in residual hardness. Human and LLM judges differ in which summary--dimension units remain difficult, and this mismatch is strongly dimension-dependent. Consistency shows a pronounced LLM-hard shift, whereas coherence shows a human-hard shift. We further show that human-easy but LLM-hard cases are partially predictable from observable source--summary properties. These findings suggest that aggregate human alignment reflects only part of LLM-as-a-judge reliability, while psychometric residual diagnostics support more informative judge evaluation and more targeted human--LLM collaboration.

items.title: Evaluating VQA in Vision Language Models using Cooperative Principles
items.abstract: We evaluate the performance of Vision Language Models in Visual Question Answering (VQA) when questions violate Grice's maxims. To do this, we use VLMs to generate question modifiers that add non-essential, ambiguous or false information and show that in the presence of such violations, the VLMs that we evaluate (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Llava) show diminished performance. Further, we empirically show the difference between how humans reason pragmatically compared to VLMs, and the difference in VLM reasoning when it resolves violations that are human-induced compared to those that are AI-generated. Finally, we show that human cognitive effort (measured through time-on-task in an experiment) is lower for resolving VLM-induced violations, but VLMs themselves perform less accurately in such cases.

items.title: Evaluator-in-the-Loop Monte Carlo Tree Search via LLM Agents for Motif Scaffolding in Protein Design
items.abstract: Motif-scaffolding systems commonly follow a generate-then-filter paradigm, in which candidate proteins are generated independently and structural evaluation is used primarily for terminal screening or ranking. This paradigm underuses evaluation: failed predictions contain state-specific evidence about whether a design requires repair of motif geometry, global foldability, or other structural constraints. We introduce \textbf{ELMS} (Evidence-based LLM-guided Monte Carlo Search), an evaluator-in-the-loop search framework for motif scaffolding that turns such evaluator feedback into targeted design actions. Effective reuse of structural feedback is nontrivial because different scaffold states exhibit different failure modes, and repeatedly refining a single trajectory can prematurely commit computation to an unproductive region of sequence space. ELMS therefore retains evaluated scaffolds as persistent search states: a Critic Agent diagnoses state-local structural failures, a Policy Agent selects targeted operators with execution parameters, motif-locked operators realize legal sequence modifications, and MCTS determines which historical states should receive further design effort. Under the standard GeomMotif protocol (100 candidates per task), ELMS achieves Successful rates of 86.41\% on single-motif tasks and 84.57\% on paired-motif tasks, exceeding the strongest prior baseline by 19.3 and 21.9 percentage points, respectively. On MotifBench, under a matched 100-candidate search budget, it solves 26.7 of 30 tasks on average (88.89\% Task Success), compared with 16.0 tasks (53.33\%) for the strongest baseline. These results establish ELMS as an effective approach for converting structural evaluation from a terminal filter into actionable guidance for iterative motif scaffolding.

items.title: EVOL: Simulator-Guided Evolutionary Expert Synthesis for Deployment-Free Learning Path Recommendation
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for learning path recommendation (LPR) faces two coupled obstacles. First, the policy must commit to a sequence of L concepts without intermediate feedback, producing a combinatorial search space that grows super-exponentially with L and provides reward only at the final step. Second, expert learning paths would be the natural cure for sparse-reward RL, but they do not exist in educational data, because student logs record what learners did, not what they should have done. We address both obstacles by importing a recipe from simulator-based demonstration learning in robotics: the knowledge tracing simulator is used both to synthesize per-learner expert demonstrations through evolutionary search and to train a deployment-free policy that distills these demonstrations into a feed-forward learner. Our framework, EVOL, instantiates this pipeline with an asymmetric actor-critic where the actor commits to deployment-realistic blind planning while the critic exploits the privileged simulator state during training. Across three datasets (ASSIST15, Junyi, and EdNet; 39-189 concepts) and path lengths L = 5, 10, and 20, EVOL surpasses 8 baselines spanning heuristic, sequential, RL, graph-enhanced RL, and LLM-enhanced methods. We further compare three imitation strategies (BC, AWR, and DAPG) and show that final performance is governed by the quality of evolutionary experts rather than by the particular imitation objective.

items.title: Evolutionary Computation for Trustworthy AI: From Attacks and Defenses to Self-Evolving Era
items.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) has evolved from task-specific models to foundation models and agents, the scope of trustworthy AI has expanded from model-level robustness to the reliability and safety of broader AI systems. This evolution has also expanded the attack surface from individual models to broader system-level interactions, including tool use, context, and interaction trajectories with dynamic environments. As a result, maintaining reliable and safe behavior under changing or deliberately manipulated conditions has become increasingly challenging. The search for effective attacks and defenses often relies on black-box feedback to navigate discrete choices among words, actions, system components, or their combinations. Multiple objectives and expensive candidate evaluations further limit what can be explored. Evolutionary Computation (EC), with its population-based, gradient-free search and flexible variation and selection mechanisms, is well suited to these settings. This survey reviews how EC has been applied to trustworthy AI across three directions: evolutionary attacks, evolutionary defenses, and trustworthy self-evolving AI systems. Unlike prior reviews that treat trustworthy AI, EC, and self-evolving systems largely separately, we connect these lines through a common evolutionary perspective. For self-evolving AI, we examine how trustworthiness governs the generation and retention of updates that shape subsequent adaptation. We further synthesize evaluation methods and benchmark resources from both trustworthiness and evolutionary-search perspectives. Finally, we discuss key challenges and future research directions toward more effective and reliable use of EC in trustworthy AI.

items.title: EvoRiskBench: An Evolving Benchmark for Runtime Security Risks in Workspace Agents
items.abstract: Workspace agents combine large language models with execution harnesses to perform stateful, multi-step tasks that access or modify external resources. Existing benchmarks leave gaps in executable coverage of their runtime security risks, while evolving model capabilities, harnesses, tools, and threats motivate benchmark evolution. We introduce EvoRiskBench, an evolving benchmark organized around the EP-Path-EF framework, which links an initial risk entry point to a one-hop technical effect through an agent-mediated risk path. The framework defines nine entry-point categories and five effect categories; a 20-participant study supports their interpretability and classification consistency on representative cases. Guided by this framework, an automated end-to-end workflow constructs and executes risk cases in isolated environments and independently verifies outcomes using runtime traces and environment states. The benchmark provides a reproducible dataset of 450 adversarial tasks across six scenarios. We evaluate nine model-harness configurations spanning three models (GPT-5.6 Sol, DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, and Claude Opus 5) and three harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw). Our results reveal substantial vulnerabilities across systems. The most vulnerable configuration, Codex with DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, reaches a 68.44% attack success rate (ASR), indicating that configuration of workspace agent is insufficient to ensure secure autonomous execution. ASR varies more across models than harnesses, and harness differences depend on the model. The benchmark cases and evaluation platform will be released after completion of artifact safety and reproducibility checks.

items.title: Experimental Evaluation of Croton Megalocarpus Oil as a Bio-Based Cutting Fluid in Turning Inconel 718 Alloys
items.abstract: The use of conventional petroleum-based cutting fluids poses significant environmental and occupational health concerns, highlighting the need for biodegradable alternatives in modern manufacturing. Exposure to cutting-fluid mists and volatile compounds generated during machining can cause respiratory irritation, skin disorders, and asthma. This study investigated the performance of Croton megalocarpus oil as a bio-based cutting fluid for machining Inconel 718. The performance of three cutting fluids was compared: conventional mineral cutting oil, filtered Croton megalocarpus base oil, and Croton megalocarpus oil containing 0.5 wt% graphene nanoparticles. Turning experiments were conducted on a TSL-550D precision lathe under identical machining conditions for all three fluids. The results showed that pure Croton oil reduced the cutting temperature to 160 ℃, representing a 5.3% reduction compared with mineral oil (169 ℃). The graphene-enhanced Croton oil provided the greatest reduction in cutting temperature, with a mean value of 136 ℃, corresponding to a 19.5% reduction relative to mineral oil. It also produced the lowest surface roughness (1.68 μm), compared with 1.72 μm for pure Croton oil and 1.70 μm for mineral oil. These results indicate that graphene-enhanced Croton megalocarpus oil has potential as a bio-based alternative to conventional mineral cutting fluids for machining Inconel 718.

items.title: Explainable AI and Governance
items.abstract: To have an efficient artificial intelligence (AI) governance in the world that is characterised by increased auto-automation, it is vital to navigate the emergence of explainable AI (XAI). Since AI systems are used for making important decisions in fields as diverse as the financial industry or healthcare, their complexity (often due to the fact that they can be labelled as black boxes) becomes a critical burden when it comes to accountability, trust, and compliance with regulatory forces. This chapter discusses the role of XAI methods, which are supposed to make the reasoning of AI clear and comprehensible, as a key connection between technical AI-building and sound and ethical governance models. Explainability is not only an objective that is pursued at a technical level but also a socio-legal requirement. We explore the existing terrain, exploring and identifying various XAI solutions, including local and global explanations and model-agnostic and model-specific, and evaluating their potential usability by different interested parties, including regulators, system developers, and the impacted population. One of the main themes is the ability of explainability to be codified and go beyond the broad principles to provide quantifiable and enforceable benchmarks of algorithmic fairness and human control. Finally, to govern effectively, there needs to be explainability into the lifecycle of AI development in order to completely balance the element of power, preserve the trust of people, and be able to deliver an evenly distributed promise of AI in order to create a technology-friendly human-centred existence.

items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence For Real-Time Cyber Attack Detection And Risk Assessment
items.abstract: Security operations centers rely on machine learning in increasing amounts when conducting network intrusion detection, but the inability to comprehend, trust, and act on alerts caused by black-box models is a significant issue under time pressure. Explainable AI (XAI) solutions such as SHAP and LIME provide solutions to the transparency problem, yet the explanation latency that they introduce makes them unsuitable for real-time triage of security alerts. This paper introduces an integrated XAI framework that consists of a Random Forest-XGBoost soft voting model along with a latency-aware dual mode explanation engine that uses the optimal LIME path for real-time query explanation and the approximated KernelSHAP path for forensic query explanation. A feature weighted risk scoring component transforms explanation attribution scores into a risk score bound in real time. Using the UNSW-NB15 dataset, we show that the framework provides state-of-the-art detection performance comparable to black box baselines with explanation latency well within real-time bounds and high attribution stability for forensic purposes.

items.title: Exploring ChatGPT as a Consumer Decision Tool for Restaurant Selection in Indonesia
items.abstract: The growing use of artificial intelligence in consumer decision-making has changed the way consumers search for, evaluate, and purchase hospitality services. In Jakarta, where dining options are diverse and highly competitive, this study examines how trust and social influence shape consumers' decisions to use ChatGPT for restaurant recommendations. Data were collected from 322 respondents who had used ChatGPT for restaurant selection and analyzed using PLS-SEM in SmartPLS. Trust has a positive and substantial effect on decision-making, indicating that users are more willing to follow ChatGPT's suggestions when they believe it is credible, dependable, and useful. Social influence also has a positive effect, indicating that peer encouragement, social approval, and the normalization of AI use increase reliance on ChatGPT. Together the two constructs explain 67.5 percent of the variance in decision-making, offering insight for restaurant operators, AI developers, and digital marketers in emerging markets.

items.title: Exploring Dragging Interaction on Curved Displays in Virtual Reality
items.abstract: As virtual reality (VR) environments increasingly incorporate curved displays, dragging interactions on such displays have become more common. However, evidence on how display geometry affects dragging remains limited. We examined dragging performance and subjective workload using controller-based ray casting in two repeated-measures experiments with 12 participants each. Experiment 1 used curvilinear measurements, whereas Experiment 2 used angular measurements. Both manipulated display curvature, viewing depth, target amplitude and width. The results show that, compared with flat displays, curved displays with specific curvature settings yielded shorter movement times, lower error rates, and lower subjective workload. Increasing depth reduced movement time under curvilinear measurement but increased it under angular measurement. We further evaluated existing Fitts’ law adaptations and proposed an extension of the two-part model that incorporates display curvature. These findings inform the design and modeling of dragging interactions on curved VR displays.

items.title: Exploring Human–AI Collaboration and Strategic Decision-Making in UAE Government Institutions: Reconfiguring Leadership and Human Judgement in the
items.abstract: This study investigates human–AI collaboration and strategic decision-making in UAE government institutions, examining how artificial intelligence is transforming leadership practices, decision processes and human judgement. Although AI is integral to the UAE’s digital government transformation, existing research has focused mainly on technological adoption, organisational performance and digital transformation, leaving limited understanding of how human–AI collaboration reconfigures strategic decision-making and leadership responsibilities. The study addresses this gap by examining the relationship between human judgement and AI-enabled decision support, the effects of collaboration on strategic decision-making and organisational transformation, and emerging leadership challenges in AI-enabled governance. An exploratory qualitative research design was employed, drawing on academic literature, policy documents, official government publications and other documentary sources. The data were analysed thematically, guided by Dynamic Capabilities Theory, to identify patterns related to collaboration, decision-making, leadership transformation and human judgement. Findings show that AI is moving strategic decision-making towards collaborative arrangements in which AI provides analytical capabilities, predictive insights and decision support, while human leaders retain responsibility for contextual interpretation, ethical reasoning and final judgement. The study contributes by extending understanding of AI-enabled leadership through a human–AI collaboration perspective, demonstrating how technological capabilities and human judgement can be integrated within government decision processes. It concludes that effective AI governance requires complementarity rather than leadership displacement. Future research should examine these dynamics through empirical studies involving government leaders and employees across different UAE institutions and comparative public-sector contexts and broader institutional outcomes. The study recommends strengthening AI literacy, leadership capabilities, institutional readiness and responsible governance.

items.title: Exploring suicide among immigrant farmworkers in the United States: evidence from the National Violent Death Reporting System
items.abstract: Background Agricultural workers face some of the highest suicide rates in the United States, yet limited research has examined suicide among immigrant and migrant farmworkers (IMFs), a population recognized as particularly vulnerable within occupational health surveillance priorities. This study examined circumstances contributing to suicide among IMFs and compared these to circumstances among U.S.-born farmworkers using National Violent Death Reporting System (NVDRS) data. Methods This multiple methods study used NVDRS data from 2013 to 2023, restricted to decedents in agricultural worker occupations (SOC Minor Group 45–2000) who died by suicide. Decedents were classified as IMFs (foreign-born) or U.S.-born based on birthplace. Bivariate analyses examined associations between nativity and reported circumstances preceding suicide, followed by multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, race, ethnicity, marital status, and education. A single-author qualitative analysis of investigative narratives, using an iterative inductive coding process with peer debriefing as a rigor check, identified themes describing IMF suicide circumstances. Results Of 1,162 decedents, 17% ( n = 201) were foreign-born. IMFs were older, more likely male, more likely Hispanic, and had lower educational attainment than U.S.-born decedents. IMFs were less likely to die by firearm (22% vs. 57%) and more likely to die by hanging/strangulation/suffocation (64% vs. 30%). In adjusted analysis, Hispanic ethnicity (OR = 0.014), older age (OR = 0.961), and being married (OR = 0.366) were associated with lower odds, while firearm method (OR = 2.126) was associated with higher odds, of U.S.-born status. Investigative documentation completeness did not differ significantly by nativity. Qualitative analysis identified four themes: stigma and avoidance of mental health care; violent and conflictual intimate relationships; substance use and associated familial shame; and immigration-related vulnerability and compounded isolation. Conclusion IMFs experience intersectional stressors—including immigration-related vulnerability, stigma, and isolation—that shape suicide risk in ways distinct from U.S.-born farmworkers, and that align with constructs of thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness from the Interpersonal-Psychological Theory of Suicide. Predominant use of hanging/strangulation among IMFs highlights limitations of conventional lethal means restriction strategies for this population. Culturally responsive, community-based, and workplace interventions—including stigma reduction, social connection programming, and multilingual lethal means safety messaging—are needed to address suicide risk among this underrecognized and vulnerable occupational group.

items.title: Family-Supported Personal Hygiene Education for Improving Dermatitis-Related Knowledge Among Agricultural Workers: A Case Study
items.abstract: Dermatitis is a common occupational health concern among agricultural workers, who are frequently exposed to environmental irritants, pesticides, fertilizers, plants, and prolonged sunlight exposure. Inadequate knowledge and suboptimal personal hygiene practices may further increase the risk of persistent skin problems. This study aimed to describe the application of personal hygiene health education, combined with family-supported mentoring, to address a knowledge deficit in a farmer with dermatitis. A case study design was conducted in the working area of the Padang Community Health Center involving a 53-year-old sugarcane farm laborer and her family. The intervention was implemented over seven consecutive days. It consisted of four visits, two structured educational sessions focused on recognizing dermatitis and appropriate personal hygiene practices, and continuous family-supported mentoring. Knowledge was assessed using pre-intervention and post-intervention questionnaires, while relevant behavioral responses were documented throughout the intervention period. The participant demonstrated several misconceptions about dermatitis and suboptimal hygiene practices at baseline, including delayed bathing, inconsistent handwashing, and reusing field clothing. Following the intervention, the knowledge score increased from 72.5 to 90, indicating improved understanding of dermatitis and recommended personal hygiene practices. Family-supported educational mentoring was associated with improved knowledge and may represent a feasible nursing approach to strengthening self-management of dermatitis among agricultural workers. Larger studies using validated instruments, comparative designs, and longer follow-up periods are required to evaluate the effectiveness and sustainability of this intervention.

items.title: FastOPD: On-Policy Distillation for Lightweight VLA Deployment
items.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models have scaled rapidly to enhance manipulation performance and generalizability, but this scaling incurs high computational costs that render real-world deployment increasingly challenging. Existing approaches typically mitigate this issue by designing smaller architectures or reducing the iterative denoising steps in flow-based policies. In this work, we propose FastOPD, a foundation-to-lightweight VLA framework that enables the practical deployment of large-scale VLAs through efficient on-policy distillation. Specifically, FastOPD adapts a flow map for single-state teacher supervision and combines it with a self-consistency objective to construct a compact student that learns the teacher dynamics. Furthermore, we theoretically demonstrate that minimizing this objective allows the distilled student to recover a distribution on par with that induced by an ideal few-step teacher model. We evaluate FastOPD across diverse foundation policies in simulation and real-world experiments. On LIBERO, FastOPD retains 84% of the performance of $π_{0.5}$ with only two inference steps, reducing inference latency by 78.1% while outperforming existing few-step distillation baselines in average success rate. With LingBot-VLA as the teacher, FastOPD improves the single-step success rate over the base student by 15.9 percentage points on RoboTwin 2.0. We further demonstrate its applicability to a World Action Model (WAM) and deploy a compact student distilled from MolmoAct2 on a real robot.

items.title: Feasibility and expert evaluation of a medical large language model in an interdisciplinary clinical board
items.abstract: Abstract Interdisciplinary clinical boards (ICB) on chronic inflammatory diseases discuss complicated and multidisciplinary cases with inflammatory conditions among experts in their discipline. Medically specialized large language models (LLMs) are finding increasingly widespread use among physicians to answer clinical questions. LLMs offer the potential to close the gap between rapidly expanding medical knowledge and limited time of physicians by providing evidence-based summaries to clinical questions and enable “real-time” literature search. However, it is unclear if LLMs can be implemented in clinical routine of ICB. In this prospective study, 100 consecutive real-world cases were discussed in our ICB. Each case was first discussed independently of the LLM and a preliminary recommendation was documented. The clinical question was then entered in the LLM “OpenEvidence”, the answer was reviewed by the board with the opportunity to add aspects not previously raised, and the recommendation was subsequently confirmed as final. Each participating expert evaluated the answer of the LLM using a questionnaire comprising eight Likert scale (1–5) items and one free-text item. Two physicians, blinded to each other, additionally evaluated outputs for their agreement with the board’s decision. The same cases were evaluated after prompt optimization at two different time points. The 100 discussed cases resulted in 759 rater-case evaluations. A mean of 2.3 specialties were directly involved in each case. The highest score was achieved by the item “OpenEvidence provided clinically relevant information for this case.” (4.06). Recommendation for future use achieved a mean score of 3.95. Complete agreement of the LLM answer with the final recommendation of the ICB was rated in 40.2% and 50.5% of all evaluable cases ( n = 97) by the two raters. When restricted to consensus cases, i.e. cases rated identically by both raters ( n = 62 of 97), complete agreement was 51.6%. Outputs after prompt optimization tended to be associated with higher agreement, but did not reach statistical significance. Outputs were not stable over time. The integration of OpenEvidence into an ICB was feasible and was perceived as useful by the participating specialists, with partial or complete concordance with the final board recommendation in the majority of evaluable cases. As the study did not assess patient outcomes, clinical harm or hallucinations, no conclusions on patient safety can be drawn. The LLM was naturally limited by the information provided in the prompt. Inadequate questions or missing information led to suboptimal answers, highlighting the importance of identifying and including relevant information beforehand. Expert oversight remains essential. Model drift of LLMs may outweigh prompt optimization.

items.title: Feature-Driven Framework for Interpretable Detection and Analysis of Android Malware Through Network and Application Behaviors
items.abstract: This paper presents a complete framework for feature-driven Android malware detection that combines predictive modeling with explainable artificial intelligence to improve classification accuracy, interpretability, and operational dependability. The system initiates by examining network-flow metrics, including Source Port (SP), Initial Window Bytes Forward (IW), packet rates, and user activity indicators, derived from a publicly accessible dataset including 355,630 cases across four classifications: Adware, Scareware, SMS malware, and benign. Feature preprocessing utilizes the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) analysis to eliminate multicollinearity to discern the most important variables, hence assuring a non-redundant and highly relevant feature collection. Subsequently, Gradient Boosting Classifier (XGBC) and Decision Tree Classifier (DTC) are augmented with metaheuristic optimization algorithms, Tailor Optimization Algorithm (TOA) and Spotted Deer Optimization Algorithm (SDOA), to boost convergence, stability, and generalization. Model interpretability is attained by Delta-XAI, which identifies SP, IW, and User Interaction/Write operations as the principal features, collectively representing approximately 80% of the explanatory power of the top features. Assessment by five-fold cross-validation indicates that the XGBC+TOA (XGTO) configuration attains an overall accuracy of 98.0%, exhibiting excellent precision and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), surpassing all other models. This framework combines feature-centric selection, enhanced learning, and explainable AI to deliver a dependable, interpretable, and pragmatic approach for identifying Android malware, thereby connecting data-driven analysis with practical cybersecurity implementations.

items.title: Few-Shot Remote Sensing Scene Classification Leveraging Collaboration of Foundation Models
items.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable generalization ability for few-shot learning (FSL). However, their potential for remote sensing scene classification has not been fully explored. Existing methods mainly adapt a single vision–language model and seldom exploit the complementary strengths of different foundation models. Moreover, the inconsistency between visual and textual representations limits the effectiveness of cross-modal learning under limited supervision. To address these issues, we propose a framework for few-shot remote sensing scene classification leveraging collaboration of foundation models. Specifically, the proposed framework integrates a large language model, a text-to-image diffusion model, and a vision–language model to enrich class semantics, synthesize category-related training samples, and learn transferable visual-textual representations. Furthermore, a Deep Cross-modal Alignment (DCA) module is developed to improve feature consistency across modalities. The DCA module incorporates multi-scale visual features, lightweight adapters, and a contrastive learning objective to obtain more discriminative task-adaptive representations. Extensive experiments on 12 remote sensing scene classification datasets under various few-shot settings demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance compared with existing prompt learning and efficient parameter tuning methods, with consistent improvements observed on average across the evaluated datasets. Recent multimodal large language models evaluated in the zero-shot setting are additionally reported as references, while the 2-shot results of our method illustrate the performance when limited labeled data are available. This comparison provides a broader view of the trade-offs between label availability, classification accuracy, and inference cost across the two paradigms.

items.title: FiberGeoText: A Vision-Language Model for Population- Level Organization of Superficial White Matter
items.abstract: The superficial white matter (SWM), a critical brain region for cognition across the lifespan and brain disease, contains abundant short-range association fibers whose organization remains incompletely characterized, in part because the short trajectories and highly variable cortical folding make correspondence across individuals challenging. Anatomically corresponding connections may vary in spatial location across individuals and therefore may not be adequately defined by geometric proximity alone. We introduce FiberGeoText (FGT), a vision-language model (VLM) for organizing short-range superficial white matter (SWM) streamlines reconstructed from ultra-high-resolution diffusion MRI into population-level clusters. FGT jointly represents three complementary properties of each streamline: its three-dimensional trajectory, its cortical anatomical context, and its shape. Cortical endpoint information from multiple parcellation schemes is expressed as text and encoded using a pretrained large language model (LLM), enabling heterogeneous anatomical descriptions to contribute to a common continuous representation. We evaluated FGT on acquired submillimeter 0.76 mm diffusion MRI data. Compared with state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, FGT produced substantially greater cortical parcel coherence, within-cluster shape consistency, cluster-size consistency, and cross-subject correspondence. The trained model also generalizes well to unseen subjects with an average of 96.7% of the 5,000 learned clusters recovered, and high consistency of cluster structure between training and testing data. Together, these findings demonstrate that integrating geometric, anatomical, and shape information by learning multimodal deep embeddings with a VLM model enables robust learning of population-consistent SWM organization despite interindividual anatomical variability.

items.title: Fifteen Lessons Learned from Designing, Evaluating, and Deploying a Contextual Virtual Reality Fire Safety Trainer: The FireGuard Case Study
items.abstract: Conventional fire-safety awareness campaigns built on brochures, leaflets, and instructional videos have shown limited success in developing transferable hazard-recognition skills, and simply moving this content into a virtual reality (VR) headset does not resolve the problem. This Project Report synthesizes fifteen cross-cutting lessons learned from a three-phase FireGuard case study conducted in Dubai and Sharjah, spanning a 149-resident needs-assessment survey, an expert-validated True-Context (TContext) game design, and an 80-participant controlled experiment in which the contextual group achieved higher learning gains and outperformed a non-contextual VR baseline on usability, engagement, and motivation. Rather than presenting new experimental data, this report integrates findings from three reported phases into a single cross-phase account and an accompanying six-layer evaluation architecture. The fifteen lessons are organized into three clusters. The Phase 1 survey yields three diagnostic lessons that show a clear distinction. Awareness is not preparedness. Passive delivery persists for cost reasons, not effectiveness. Training access remains structurally unequal and employer-dependent. The TContext framework and Phase 2 expert review yield a further set of design lessons: Passive content does not become contextual simply by appearing inside a headset, Contextual design - more than immersion alone, was associated with the larger learning gains observed. These design lessons also point to the need for explicit temporal and situational escalation. Distributed situational awareness and progressive interactivity should be built into scenario design. Gamification should function as a teaching tool rather than a descriptive layer. Structured, multi-domain expert review before user trials is likewise associated with reduced redesign costs. Phase 3 and the integrative discussion yield five lessons on evaluation and deployment. Balance interaction realism against accessibility for non-technical users. Sustain motivation through real-time, scenario-anchored feedback. Isolate the independent variable through rigorous experimental design. Adopt a six-layer evaluation architecture, spanning reach to durable behaviour change. Data quality is shaped through field logistics and human factors. Together, these fifteen lessons offer practical, theory-grounded guidance. They are intended for researchers, safety educators, and policymakers designing similar VR interventions in other high-density, multilingual urban settings. However, their transferability beyond the present study has not been directly tested.

items.title: Figuring GenAI: Toward a Technocurious Framework for History Education
items.abstract: Background: GenAI has entered education rapidly, intensifying debates about pedagogy, authority, ethics, and disciplinary integrity. In history education, these tensions are especially pronounced because GenAI can support access, scaffolding, and experimentation while also flattening interpretation, obscuring evidence, and reproducing dominant narratives. Focus of Study: This conceptual paper introduces technocuriosity as a methodological and pedagogical stance for history educators, teacher educators, and researchers engaging GenAI in practice. Situated in conversation with postdigital and speculative scholarship in education, technocuriosity approaches GenAI as an emergent, sociotechnical problem space best studied through recursive, critical experimentation. Research Design: We develop a four-part framework centered on configuration, figures, liveness, and speculative futures, and use these layers to trace the conditions under which GenAI is introduced, negotiated, resisted, or incorporated in history classrooms. We then outline the methodological commitments that follow from this stance, including recursive prompting, persona work, shadow archives, and classroom experimentation. Conclusions: Technocuriosity offers a way to engage GenAI with curiosity disciplined by historical thinking, ethical scrutiny, and attention to power, while keeping inquiry, interpretation, and evidence at the center of history education.

items.title: Follow the Winners: Conservative Policy Improvement with the Cross-Entropy Method for Critic-Free RFT
items.abstract: Critic-free reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) for agentic large language models is often done through GRPO-style methods, which compute a group baseline over repeated rollouts to reduce target variance. However, this setup is ill-suited to agents acting in stateful environments such as live services or security sandboxes, where repeated rollouts are impractical to obtain and aggressive updates entrench the noise of long, sparsely verified trajectories. We propose \textit{Follow the Winners} (FTW), a critic-free policy-learning algorithm that adapts the cross-entropy method to RFT, replacing group rollouts with an ordinal filter on replay-buffer samples that yields polynomial concentration in the order statistic of returns. We derive FTW through a control-as-inference lens, which also recovers GRPO and DPO as specific modelling choices, identifying GRPO as risk-neutral while DPO and FTW share a bounded risk-seeking offset that FTW controls. We identify this offset as an inherent trade-off of variance reduction through ordinal filters on samples, whereas a critic model induces a different trade-off between bias and variance. Scaled to agentic LLM post-training, FTW matches GRPO and PPO on Sokoban and Search-R1 baselines, showing a viable trade-off from a value model or group rollouts to CPU memory.

items.title: Frequency Is Not Sensitivity Identifying Safety-Sensitive Experts in Sparse MoE LLM
items.abstract: Suppressing a small set of routed experts can weaken the safety behavior of a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model without retraining. Which experts to suppress is therefore a security question, and the usual answer is activation frequency, but frequency measures use, not influence. We test an alternative: router-gradient sensitivity, the sensitivity of the sequence loss to the gate weights that select an expert. Across five MoE architectures, we rank experts by each signal on 500 benign and 500 malicious prompts and measure refusal on 100 held-out malicious prompts under two budgets: equal expert counts and equal nominal malicious routing traffic (1%-5%). Under each of the two budgets, router-gradient selection reduces refusals more than activation in 24 of 25 conditions, and more than a ten-trial random mean in all 25. The largest effect is in OLMoE, where refusals fall from 34 to 9 of 100 prompts (73.53% relative) with no degraded outputs, indicating substantive compliance rather than broken generation. After matching expert counts in every layer, gradient selection still produces greater refusal reduction than activation in 23 of 25 conditions, with two ties. An exploratory cross-model analysis links larger malicious-versus-benign concentration gaps to greater peak gradient effects (rho = 0.90; exact two-sided p = 0.083, n = 5). Together, the results support gradient selection under the tested budgets.

items.title: From Benchmarks to Production: A Text-to-SQL System for Complex Financial Data
items.abstract: General-purpose Text-to-SQL systems achieve strong performance on academic benchmarks like Spider and BIRD, where schemas are relatively shallow and column values are often human readable. In production financial databases, where concepts are stored as opaque integer keys rather than human-readable strings, these methods fall below 50%, as even simple queries require multiple joins and filter predicates reference opaque IDs. We present Financial LINking Text-to-SQL (FLINT), a domain-specialized Text-to-SQL system that closes this gap through three key components: (1) a lookup agent that dynamically resolves natural-language concepts to question-specific reference table constraints, (2) embedding-based retrieval of structurally similar query templates from a compact, expert-authored bank, and (3) schema linking that prunes a large table schema to the relevant subset by traversing foreign-key chains, rather than relying on name similarity alone. We evaluate on two datasets totaling 359 questions over production financial schemas. FLINT outperforms various state-of-the-art baselines using the same LLM. The system is deployed in production as part of a financial data retrieval service.

items.title: From Corporate Control to Algorithmic Control: Rethinking Directors’ Duties and Liability in AI-Driven Corporations
items.abstract: Corporate governance has traditionally assumed that important company decisions are made by human directors, managers, and officers who can be questioned about the reasons for their choices. Artificial intelligence is changing that assumption. AI systems are now used to analyse markets, assess risk, screen employees, detect fraud, forecast demand, recommend investments, and in some settings take actions with little or no human intervention. The legal problem is not simply whether a company may use AI. It is whether existing rules on directors’ duties can still allocate responsibility when an important corporate decision is partly or largely produced by an algorithm. This paper examines that problem mainly through Indian company law, with comparative reference to Delaware, the United Kingdom, the European Union, the OECD and the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires directors to act in good faith, exercise due and reasonable care, skill and diligence, and use independent judgment. These duties remain relevant when AI is used. The difficulty is that the traditional idea of a director as the person who gathers information and then exercises judgment does not fit neatly where an AI system filters information, recommends an outcome, or executes the decision itself. The paper argues that AI should not become a legal excuse for directors, but directors should also not become automatic guarantors of every error made by a system they did not design or operate. Liability should instead be linked to the degree of AI autonomy, the importance of the decision, the quality of human oversight, the foreseeability of the risk, and the ability of the company and its directors to intervene. The paper proposes an AI Corporate Responsibility Framework with four levels of AI use: assistive, delegated, supervised autonomous, and high-autonomy decision systems. For each level, it proposes a different combination of board oversight, documentation, testing, human review, vendor responsibility, and director liability. The central conclusion is that the duty of directors should evolve into a clear duty of AI oversight. This duty would require directors to understand the material AI systems used by the company, identify significant risks, establish suitable controls, monitor performance, keep records of important AI-supported decisions, and intervene when a system presents a serious or foreseeable risk. Such a framework protects the basic principle of director accountability while recognising that modern corporate decisions may be produced through a network of directors, employees, software providers, data sources, and autonomous systems.

items.title: From Requirements to Attack Trees: Grounded LLM Agents for Design-Time Security Review
items.abstract: Design-level security weaknesses can arise from requirements, trust assumptions, missing controls, and data flows before implementation begins. Existing security practices often identify these issues after code is written. We present a multi-agent LLM framework for design-time security analysis from product requirement documents and architecture diagrams. The proposed framework parses architecture diagrams into graph representations, generates misuse and failure cases, constructs attack trees, checks governance and compliance gaps, recommends mitigations, assigns enterprise security-domain tags, and produces a candidate revised architecture recommendation for expert review. The framework does not retrieve from Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) databases at inference time. Instead, it analyzes system behavior, trust boundaries, component interactions, and data-flow assumptions. Misuse cases act as intermediate representations that link findings to system components and attack paths, while a validation and refinement loop filters unsupported findings and improves grounding, traceability, and actionability. We evaluate the framework on a Microsoft reference-labeled threat-modeling example, labeled synthetic PRD--architecture pairs, and two open-ended systems: Berty and Gas Town. The reference-labeled case supports threat-recovery and actionability analysis, while the open-ended cases evaluate validity, noise, traceability, actionability, redundancy, and attack-tree quality. Results show that architecture-informed, misuse-driven reasoning improves review quality compared with single-shot and ablation baselines. Keywords: LLM Multi-Agent Systems, Design-Time Security, Threat Modeling, Vulnerability Discovery, Architecture Diagrams, Security Analysis, Misuse Case Derivation, Attack Trees, Iterative Reasoning, Security Governance.

items.title: FSPO: Policy-Consistent Risk and Pareto-Feasible Control for Budgeted LLM RL Post-Training
items.abstract: Adaptive LLM reinforcement-learning post-training changes multiple training actuators online, including rollout temperature, group size, clipping, KL regularization, verifier allocation, and update budget. Three coupled issues remain unresolved. A future-risk model trained from behavior trajectories need not estimate the risk induced by the controller that will be deployed; a score calibrated on logged state-action pairs can become miscalibrated after selective action choice; and independent per-resource minimum costs do not in general certify a feasible multi-resource continuation. We introduce FSPO, a feedback-state controller for budgeted LLM RL post-training that addresses these issues jointly. FSPO learns a policy-consistent risk-to-go model whose Bellman target follows the same frozen controller used for future decisions, together with a long-horizon utility model. Decision-conditioned trajectory calibration (DCTC) calibrates risk on cross-fitted trajectories generated by actions selected by provisional controllers. A Pareto resource continuation certificate (PRCC) admits an action only when a non-dominated cumulative reservation remains feasible over the residual horizon. items.title: Future Digital Dominance: Gen Z vs. Gen AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) is rapidly becoming the dominating force in this new age, despite the fact that Generation Z has played a significant role in defining the digital culture that exists today. As a consequence of the exponential rise of digital technology, this shift of power has occurred. The generation of artificial intelligence ushers in a paradigm shift toward machines having the capacity to build, learn, and evolve on their own. This is in contrast to the well-deserved reputation that Generation Z has for technical aptitude, innovation, and dependency on digital platforms for expression and communication. The ways in which Gen AI is influencing decision- making, education, creative industries, work processes, and social behaviour are discussed in depth in this article. In this in-depth examination, you will learn about the benefits and drawbacks of the digital identity developed by Generation Z in connection to the autonomous intelligence developed by Generation AI. According to the findings of the study, the transition from Generation Z to Gen AI is more than just a shift in technology; it also represents a reevaluation of human obligations in the digital age, the nature of digital dominance, and the path that innovation will take. The purpose of this study is to highlight the ways in which Gen AI is influencing the next digital age, following in the footsteps of Generation Z. Generation Z's innovation, social media, and connection were the primary factors that contributed to the formation of digital culture. Generative artificial intelligence, on the other hand, ushers in autonomic technology that is capable of cognition, creation, and operation. This transformation, which signals a new age in which AI meets human digital skills, is expected to bring about significant changes in a variety of domains, including education, work, communication and society as a whole.

items.title: Gaps from the Reviewed Occupational Health and Safety Performance Management Literature
items.abstract: The gaps for Occupational Health and Safety (OH&S) performance management in the context of Small-Scale Contractors (SSCs) for developing countries from the reviewed literature are examined in this chapter. Two essential dimensions to OH&S performance, that is, employee well-being and provision of OH&S services, found to be often neglected in most existing frameworks, have been examined. The chapter states that sustainable OH&S performance is attained once well-being programmes that address stress, mental health, and the socio-economic challenges are considered together with more accessible, structured OH&S services where there are constrained resources. Anchoring from the International Labour Organisation (ILO) and World Health Organisation (WHO) standards and the United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goals, the discussions in this chapter depict the effects of inadequate employee well-being, which lead to absenteeism, unsafe practices, and reduced productivity. In the same vein, the availability of employee well-being significantly strengthens safety outcomes by providing for targeted interventions such as wellness programmes, counselling, ergonomic design, and stress risk assessment. Further, Affective Events Theory, the Job Demands-Resources model, and the Social Capital Theory are applied as theoretical perspectives to contextualise employee well-being and OH&S service provision as OH&S performance management determinants. In conclusion, the chapter accentuates the significance of integrating employee well-being and OH&S service provision into the OH&S performance management framework for SSCs in developing economies to improve the safety of workers, increase productivity, and enhance competitiveness.

items.title: General Decision Models: Benchmarking and Insights Beyond Jev
items.abstract: General decision models, such as Jev, have recently emerged as efficient alternatives to LLMs for structured judgment and selection. But what kinds of decisions can these models reliably make, and how does their behavior change when individual decisions are composed into larger systems? To study this, we introduce JEVal, a bilingual benchmark comprising 11,257 instances from 36 datasets across 10 application domains, and evaluate 25 model configurations spanning general decision models and generative LLMs. Our results show that (1) general decision models are most competitive when decisions can be resolved from available evidence, but weaken when they require specialist knowledge or faithful uncertainty estimation: they can often identify the most likely outcome while substantially overstating its probability. (2) In more dynamic and realistic systems involving long-horizon, multi-step interactions, the advantages of fast local decision making are offset by reliability failures at the system level. on $τ$-bench, faster local decisions reduce median episode time but lower task success as decision errors accumulate over long trajectories. (3) In large-scale social simulation, decision models approach strong generative LLMs on individual response prediction at substantially lower inference cost, yet remain weaker in user profiling and exhibit larger aggregate estimation errors and systematic bias. Finally, we propose InnerJev-4B and InnerJev-27B, which internalize an open-weight LLM's own reasoning into a single-pass first-token decision through Reasoning-to-Readout Self-Distillation, with InnerJev-27B performing on par with Jev on JEVal while answering a typical query in about 0.1 s.

items.title: General Introduction
items.abstract: In most developing countries, the majority of enterprises that constitute the small-scale contractors (SSCs) play a significant role in the construction industry, even though they are vulnerable to challenges related to occupational health and safety (OH&S). The SSCs in these regions record inordinately high rates of accidents and fatalities, which are attributed to inadequate compliance with regulatory requirements, constrained financial resources, insufficient expertise, inadequate training, and ineffective communication. These factors often lead to unreported or underreported incidents and the absence of systematic risk assessments being conducted, causing ineffective interventions and biased data. Further, bad working conditions and poorly paid and physically demanding construction projects lead to negative attitudes, thus exacerbating OH&S risks. This chapter stresses the significance of client-contractor collaboration in ensuring safety culture and the adoption of performance indicators, which are fundamental in reducing risks and optimising OH&S outcomes. The chapter gives a background on the framework developed to enhance SSCs’ capabilities in improving OH&S performance to mitigate incidents and cultivate a culture of compliance. Practical guidance for policymakers, government institutions, and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) is provided in the framework for strengthening SSCs’ capabilities of fostering safer workplaces that promote sustainable construction practices in the sub-Saharan Africa region and beyond.

items.title: Generative AI ‐Supported Creative Writing Among Primary School Students: A Study of Creative Writing Performance, Writing Self‐Efficacy, and Flow State
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into creative writing is a growing trend. However, few studies have examined primary school students' interactions with GenAI alongside their writing experiences and resulting writing products. Objectives This study compared creative writing performance, writing self‐efficacy, and flow state across GenAI‐supported, peer‐collaborative and individual writing conditions. It also descriptively examined patterns of student–AI interaction during the writing activity. Methods An experiment involved 78 primary school students in China assigned to three conditions: GenAI‐supported writing ( n = 20), peer collaboration ( n = 38; 19 pairs), and individual writing ( n = 20). Results and Conclusions Students in the GenAI‐supported writing group obtained higher creative writing performance scores than those in the peer‐collaborative and individual writing groups. Interaction analysis showed that students mainly used GenAI to generate and elaborate ideas. Among episodes with observable uptake, adapted or selective incorporation was more common than direct incorporation, and no complete GenAI response was reproduced verbatim. In addition, students in the GenAI‐supported writing group also reported higher writing self‐efficacy than those in the individual writing group, although the difference from the peer‐collaborative writing group was not significant. However, they reported the lowest flow state. Writing self‐efficacy was positively associated with creative writing performance, whereas no significant association between flow state and creative writing performance was observed in this sample. These findings suggest that GenAI may serve as a resource for developing ideas in primary school creative writing.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence and commercial sexual exploitation of children: Implications for healthcare providers
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has created new avenues for the commercial sexual exploitation of children through the creation or manipulation of sexually explicit images using a child's likeness. Such images constitute a form of child sexual abuse material (CSAM), including when they are generated or manipulated without physical contact with the child. Because this abuse may occur without the child's awareness, it can complicate recognition, disclosure, and intervention while contributing to ongoing psychological harm. When such content is produced, distributed, or monetized in exchange for anything of value, it may also constitute commercial sexual exploitation of children (CSEC), a term commonly used to describe child sex trafficking. Healthcare providers play an important role in identifying possible GAI child sexual abuse material (GAI-CSAM), supporting affected children and caregivers, and incorporating digital safety into routine care. This article highlights clinical considerations for pediatric, primary care, and mental health settings, including developmentally appropriate assessment of online experiences, caregiver education, trauma-informed response, and multidisciplinary collaboration. As generative technologies evolve, clinician awareness is essential to strengthen prevention, early intervention, and responses to technology-facilitated exploitation.

items.title: GeoScaffold: Learning Compact Geometric Latents via Reconstruction for Efficient Vision-Language Navigation
items.abstract: Recent vision-and-language navigation (VLN) systems increasingly adopt streaming Video-LLM policies that map egocentric RGB observations and instructions directly to low-level actions. Yet these policies inherit weak 3D geometric priors from 2D pretraining. Existing geometry-aware extensions charge a persistent inference-time price: depth sensors, 3D encoders, or per-step perception tool calls. We propose GeoScaffold, a geometric supervision framework that pays this price once, at training time, by internalizing geometry into the policy itself. It first learns a compact depth tokenizer on depth maps from the training trajectories and freezes it. It then fine-tunes the policy with a handful of learnable geometry query tokens, training their hidden states to reconstruct navigation-critical geometry such as depth, connectivity, and traversability. This supervision turns the query states into compact geometric latents for action decoding, and through the shared weights also internalizes geometry into the backbone's own representations. Like a scaffold, the tokenizer, target generators, and reconstruction heads are discarded after training, leaving the backbone and action interface unchanged. Extensive experiments show that GeoScaffold consistently outperforms leading vision-only navigators on continuous VLN benchmarks, offering a practical paradigm for lightweight edge deployment of spatially aware embodied navigation models.

items.abstract: Amidst the context of digital transformation and the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, moral education for university students must go beyond merely shaping character and personality; it must also address the requirements for professional ethics and responsibility within the digital environment. This study focuses on clarifying moral education based on Ho Chi Minh's ideology and the significance of applying these values to the development of highquality human resources among students at nonpublic universities. The research employs methods such as document analysis, analysis and synthesis, comparison and contrast, and systematization. The findings indicate that standards—such as loyalty to the country and devotion to the people; diligence, thrift, integrity, uprightness, and absolute impartiality; and love for humanity—along with principles like aligning words with deeds, balancing construction with destruction, and lifelong moral cultivation, remain valuable in guiding students during the digital era. The study proposes solutions regarding the innovation of educational content and methods, the creation of a digital ethical environment, and the strengthening of coordination among universities, families, businesses, and society. These measures aim to help shape students who possess moral character, professional expertise, digital competence, professional responsibility, and a spirit of dedication, thereby meeting the demands for high-quality human resource development.

items.title: Global Police Operational Competence and Education Framework (G-POCEF): A Universal Systems Architecture for Ethical, Effective, Evidence-Based Police Competence, Education, Assessment, Leadership, and Organisational Capability Across Jurisdictions
items.abstract: The Global Police Operational Competence and Education Framework (G‑POCEF) is a multidisciplinary conceptual systems framework that seeks to develop a universal architecture for understanding, developing, assessing, and sustaining police competence, professional performance, organisational capability, leadership effectiveness, legitimacy, and public safety across jurisdictions. Policing systems operate within highly diverse legal, cultural, social, political, economic, and organisational environments. Despite substantial variation in laws, governance structures, training systems, community expectations, and operational demands, police organisations worldwide face common challenges involving public safety, ethical decision making, authority, accountability, legitimacy, operational effectiveness, workforce development, leadership, and organisational adaptation. G‑POCEF seeks to identify and examine the foundational principles that may contribute to effective policing across these diverse contexts. The framework draws upon literature from policing studies, criminology, educational science, psychology, decision science, organisational behaviour, leadership research, systems theory, public administration, human factors science, resilience research, comparative institutional analysis, sociology, ethics, governance studies, and public policy. The objective is to develop an integrated architecture capable of explaining how police competence emerges, develops, and functions within complex and dynamic operational environments. G‑POCEF proposes that police competence cannot be understood solely as the possession of isolated knowledge, skills, or professional qualifications. Rather, the framework conceptualises competence as an emergent property arising from interactions among multiple domains, including legal competence, ethical competence, cognitive competence, decision-making competence, communication competence, tactical competence, emotional competence, cultural competence, adaptive competence, and leadership competence. The framework further explores how these domains interact within broader organisational, legal, societal, and institutional systems. Unlike educational models that focus exclusively on curriculum design or recruit training, G‑POCEF incorporates multiple levels of analysis, including recruit education, professional development, operational performance, organisational learning, leadership systems, institutional capability, workforce sustainability, public trust, legitimacy, accountability, governance structures, and future adaptation to technological and societal change. The framework therefore seeks to examine policing as an integrated human system operating across individual, organisational, and societal levels. A central proposition of G‑POCEF is that effective policing emerges through the dynamic interaction of competence, organisational capability, legitimacy, and environmental conditions. The framework therefore explores how competencies are developed, assessed, integrated, maintained, and translated into operational performance within different policing systems around the world. Particular attention is given to competency integration, scenario-based learning, human factors, decision making under uncertainty, organisational adaptation, leadership development, and long-term professional effectiveness. The framework also examines relationships between police competence and broader concepts including public trust, procedural justice, accountability, legitimacy, institutional effectiveness, and community outcomes. In doing so, G‑POCEF aims to create a bridge between educational systems, organisational capability, operational performance, and societal expectations. The framework is intended to generate testable hypotheses and future empirical research programmes rather than present finalised conclusions. Proposed future work may include international comparative studies, competency validation research, educational intervention evaluations, leadership development investigations, organisational capability analyses, legitimacy and trust assessments, workforce sustainability studies, and cross-jurisdictional implementation research. Expected outcomes of the project include: A formal definition of global police operational competence. A universal competency architecture for policing systems. A systems model of police performance and capability. A comparative framework for evaluating policing systems across jurisdictions. A competence-based education and development architecture. A scenario-based learning and assessment framework. A leadership and organisational capability model. A legitimacy, trust, and accountability framework. A jurisdictional adaptation model for local implementation. Explicit validation, falsification, and implementation pathways. A future international research agenda for empirical testing and refinement. G‑POCEF is positioned as a conceptual, hypothesis-generating, and evidence-informed framework. Consistent with scientific principles, all framework components remain open to modification, rejection, or refinement in response to future empirical evidence, alternative explanations, competing models, methodological developments, cultural considerations, legal differences, and operational findings. The framework does not seek to prescribe a single universal policing model, but instead aims to identify and examine the underlying principles that may contribute to ethical, effective, evidence-based policing across diverse jurisdictions and societal contexts.

Underexplicit conditions, this paper shows that a system must retain at least six roles to preservethe guarantees its task requires. Each operation has a contract: a statement of what itneeds before it can act and what it guarantees afterward. Contracts may share an effectiverole only if they can replace each other wherever either is required.The argument has three parts. First, initialization establishes the conditions needed tobegin work, while acquisition supplies task-relevant information that no permitted localsource can provide. Their different requirements and guarantees distinguish theseoperations from the work that depends on them. Second, producing an artifact does notreplace evaluating it when evaluation depends on context and production guarantees onlythe artifact. Third, assessing a result does not replace settling whether action is authorizedwhen assessment leaves that decision open. With the specified contract conditions, thesearguments distinguish every pair among six roles: initialization, production, contextualevaluation, acquisition, assessment, and authorization/closure.Applying the result requires evidence for the information gap, the necessary startingconditions, and the distinct guarantees of the contracts. items.title: Hallucination Reduction for LLM-Based Audio Understanding via Multimodal Direct Preference Optimization
items.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) are prone to hallucinating and over-relying on text priors when simultaneously presented with audio and text inputs. To mitigate these hallucinations, we propose utilizing the multimodal Direct Preference Optimization (mDPO) objective, which forces the model to ground its generation in the acoustic input by contrasting intact and distorted audio counterparts. We extend this preference learning framework to the audio domain by applying a variety of acoustic perturbations. Evaluating the Qwen2-Audio backbone across the DCASE 2025 Challenge and AH Existence datasets, we demonstrate that extending mDPO to LALMs significantly enhances temporal reasoning in the complex DCASE dataset, and improves performance on basic existence verification in the AH benchmark. We identify temporal reversal, frequency masking, and random noise as the most effective perturbations. Ultimately, our approach achieves an absolute accuracy improvement of 14.0% on the DCASE 2025 dataset and 27.4% on AH Existence.
